title: SVM I — Hard Margin & the Maximal Margin Classifier

blocks.t: From the notes
SVM, as written
SVM — Support Vector Machine.

Many lines can separate the two classes. SVM finds the line which has the
maximum margin — so it is also called a Maximal Margin
Classifier.

Only the support vectors decide the hyperplane — remove any other
point and nothing changes.

In 2D the hyperplane is a line, in 3D a plane, in $n$D it is an
$(n{-}1)$-dimensional hyperplane.

blocks.t:
Why prefer the widest street? Because the margin is a proxy for
confidence. A boundary that skims past a training point will
misclassify the next, slightly-shifted point of that class. A boundary with
room on both sides tolerates that shift. Formally, the margin bounds the
generalisation error independently of the number of dimensions — which is why
SVMs work in spaces with more features than rows, where most models drown.
Setting up the geometry

A hyperplane is $\{x : w^{T}x + b = 0\}$, where $w$ is the normal vector and
$b$ shifts it from the origin. Label the classes $y_i \in \{-1,+1\}$ (not
$\{0,1\}$ — the $\pm1$ encoding is what makes the algebra collapse).

The functional margin of point $i$ is
$\hat\gamma_i = y_i\,(w^{T}x_i + b)$. It is positive when the point is on the
correct side. But it is not a distance: replacing $(w,b)$ by $(2w,2b)$ leaves
the hyperplane unchanged yet doubles $\hat\gamma_i$.
The geometric margin divides that out:
\gamma_i = \frac{y_i (w^{T}x_i + b)}{\|w\|},
which is the true perpendicular distance from $x_i$ to the hyperplane.

To remove the scale ambiguity we simply choose the normalisation
$\min_i \hat\gamma_i = 1$: the closest points sit exactly on
$w^Tx+b=\pm1$. With that convention the two margin lines are separated by
\text{margin} = \frac{2}{\|w\|},
and every point satisfies $y_i(w^{T}x_i+b)\ \geq\ 1$.

blocks.t: The primal optimisation problem

Maximising $\frac{2}{\|w\|}$ is the same as minimising $\|w\|$, which is the
same as minimising $\frac12\|w\|^2$ — a monotone transform that makes the
objective differentiable and convex quadratic. So:

This is a convex quadratic program with linear constraints: a convex
objective over a convex feasible set. Therefore any local minimum is
the global minimum, and the solution is unique. Compare with a neural network,
where the loss surface is riddled with local optima. This uniqueness is one of
the strongest practical arguments for SVMs.

Note what is not in the objective: there is no error term at all. The
constraints already forbid every mistake. That is exactly what makes it the
hard margin — it demands perfect separation, and if none exists the
feasible set is empty and the problem has no solution.
The dual, and where "support vector" comes from
Attach a multiplier $\alpha_i \ge 0$ to each constraint and form the Lagrangian
\mathcal{L}(w,b,\alpha)=\tfrac12\|w\|^2-\sum_{i=1}^{n}\alpha_i\Big[y_i(w^Tx_i+b)-1\Big].
Stationarity gives

\frac{\partial \mathcal L}{\partial w}=0 \Rightarrow
 w=\sum_i \alpha_i y_i x_i,
\qquad
\frac{\partial \mathcal L}{\partial b}=0 \Rightarrow
 \sum_i \alpha_i y_i = 0 .
Substituting back eliminates $w$ and $b$ entirely and leaves the dual:
Two consequences, both enormous
1. Sparsity. The KKT complementary-slackness condition says
\alpha_i\Big[y_i(w^Tx_i+b)-1\Big]=0 .

So for every point, either $\alpha_i=0$, or the point sits exactly on the
margin, $y_i(w^Tx_i+b)=1$. Points strictly inside their own side have
$\alpha_i=0$ and drop out of $w=\sum_i \alpha_i y_i x_i$ completely. The
survivors — the ones with $\alpha_i>0$ — are the support vectors.
This is precisely the notes' claim that only the support vectors decide the
hyperplane, and the right panel of the first figure confirms it numerically.

2. The data appears only as inner products $\langle x_i,x_j\rangle$.
Nowhere in the dual does an individual $x_i$ appear alone. Replace that inner
product with a kernel $K(x_i,x_j)$ and you get a nonlinear SVM without ever
computing the transformed features. That is Topic 74, and it is only possible
because of the dual.

Recovering $b$. From any support vector $s$,
$y_s(w^Tx_s+b)=1 \Rightarrow b = y_s - w^Tx_s$ (using $y_s^2=1$). In practice
one averages this over all support vectors for numerical stability.
Where the hard margin breaks

blocks.t: Two fatal weaknesses of the hard margin.

Infeasibility. If the classes overlap even by a single point, no $(w,b)$
satisfies all constraints. The optimiser does not return a poor answer — it
returns no answer. Real data is essentially never linearly separable.

Zero noise tolerance. Every constraint is absolute, so a single
mislabelled or outlying point can rotate the boundary arbitrarily far, as the
middle panel shows. The margin shrinks towards zero and generalisation
collapses.

Both are fixed by allowing controlled violations — slack variables and the
$C$ parameter — which is Topic 73. Non-separability caused by shape
rather than noise is fixed by kernels, Topic 74.

There is no true hard-margin implementation in scikit-learn. You approximate it
with SVC(kernel="linear", C=1e10): a huge $C$ makes violations so
expensive that the solver reproduces the hard-margin solution whenever one
exists. On non-separable data it will still return something — a soft-margin
fit with a tiny margin — rather than reporting infeasibility.
Code

import numpy as np
from sklearn.svm import SVC
from sklearn.datasets import make_blobs
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline

X, y = make_blobs(n_samples=60, centers=2, cluster_std=1.05, random_state=6)

# ==================================================================
# 1. HARD MARGIN via a huge C
# ==================================================================
clf = SVC(kernel="linear", C=1e10).fit(X, y)
w, b = clf.coef_[0], clf.intercept_[0]
print("w =", w.round(3), " b =", round(b, 3))
print("margin width 2/||w|| =", round(2 / np.linalg.norm(w), 4))

# The support vectors, and the duals
print("n support vectors:", clf.n_support_)      # per class
print("support indices  :", clf.support_)
print("dual coefs a_i*y_i:", clf.dual_coef_.round(3))
# NOTE: sklearn stores alpha_i * y_i together, so signs encode the class.

# Verify w = sum_i alpha_i y_i x_i  -- the stationarity condition
w_rebuilt = (clf.dual_coef_ @ clf.support_vectors_).ravel()
print("rebuilt w matches:", np.allclose(w, w_rebuilt))

# Verify every support vector sits exactly on a margin line: y(wx+b) == 1
fm = y[clf.support_] * (clf.support_vectors_ @ w + b)
print("functional margins of SVs:", fm.round(6))   # all 1.0

# Verify NON-support vectors are strictly outside: y(wx+b) > 1
mask = np.ones(len(X), bool); mask[clf.support_] = False
print("min functional margin of the rest:",
      round((y[mask] * (X[mask] @ w + b)).min(), 4))     # > 1

# ==================================================================
# 2. THE HEADLINE CLAIM: ONLY SUPPORT VECTORS MATTER
# ==================================================================
sv_only = SVC(kernel="linear", C=1e10).fit(clf.support_vectors_, y[clf.support_])
print("same hyperplane:", np.allclose(sv_only.coef_[0] / np.linalg.norm(sv_only.coef_[0]),
                                      w / np.linalg.norm(w), atol=1e-3))

# ...and deleting a non-support vector changes nothing
keep = np.ones(len(X), bool); keep[np.where(mask)[0][0]] = False
dropped = SVC(kernel="linear", C=1e10).fit(X[keep], y[keep])
print("unchanged after dropping a non-SV:",
      np.allclose(dropped.coef_[0], w, atol=1e-3))

# ==================================================================
# 3. SOLVING THE DUAL DIRECTLY WITH cvxopt-STYLE QP (here: scipy)
#    max  sum(a) - 0.5 * a^T Q a     with Q_ij = y_i y_j <x_i,x_j>
#    s.t. a >= 0,  sum(a_i y_i) = 0
# ==================================================================
from scipy.optimize import minimize
K = X @ X.T                             # the linear kernel / Gram matrix
Q = np.outer(y_pm := np.where(y == 1, 1.0, -1.0), y_pm) * K

def neg_dual(a):
    return 0.5 * a @ Q @ a - a.sum()
def neg_dual_grad(a):
    return Q @ a - np.ones_like(a)

res = minimize(neg_dual, np.zeros(len(X)), jac=neg_dual_grad, method="SLSQP",
               bounds=[(0, None)] * len(X),
               constraints=[{"type": "eq",
                             "fun": lambda a: a @ y_pm,
                             "jac": lambda a: y_pm}],
               options={"maxiter": 500, "ftol": 1e-12})
alpha = res.x
sv = alpha > 1e-6
print("dual found", sv.sum(), "support vectors; sklearn found", len(clf.support_))

w_dual = ((alpha * y_pm)[sv] @ X[sv])
b_dual = np.mean(y_pm[sv] - X[sv] @ w_dual)
print("w from dual:", w_dual.round(3), " (sklearn:", w.round(3), ")")

# ==================================================================
# 4. DISTANCE TO THE BOUNDARY, AND PREDICTION
# ==================================================================
# decision_function returns w.x + b  -- the FUNCTIONAL margin.
# Divide by ||w|| to get the true GEOMETRIC distance in feature units.
f = clf.decision_function(X)
geometric = f / np.linalg.norm(w)
print("closest point is", round(np.abs(geometric).min(), 4), "units away")
print("prediction = sign(w.x + b):", np.array_equal(clf.predict(X), (f > 0).astype(int)))

# ==================================================================
# 5. ALWAYS SCALE
# ==================================================================
# ||w||^2 is measured in feature units, so a feature with a huge range
# dominates the objective exactly as it dominates a distance in KNN.
svm = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), SVC(kernel="linear", C=1.0))
svm.fit(X, y)
Everything on one page
Summary

The idea: among all separating hyperplanes, take the one with the
widest empty street on either side. Wider margin = more confident = better
generalisation.

The geometry: label $y\in\{-1,+1\}$; fix the scale so the closest
points satisfy $y_i(w^Tx_i+b)=1$; then the street width is $2/\|w\|$.

The problem:
$\min \frac12\|w\|^2$ subject to $y_i(w^Tx_i+b)\ge1$ — a convex QP with a
unique global optimum.

The dual:
$\max_\alpha \sum\alpha_i-\frac12\sum\sum \alpha_i\alpha_j y_iy_j\langle x_i,x_j\rangle$
with $\alpha_i\ge0$, $\sum\alpha_iy_i=0$. It gives us two things: sparsity
(only support vectors have $\alpha_i>0$, by complementary slackness) and inner
products only (which the kernel trick will exploit).

Recover: $w=\sum_i\alpha_iy_ix_i$, $b=y_s-w^Tx_s$ for any support
vector $s$. Predict $\operatorname{sign}(w^Tx+b)$.

Fails when: classes overlap (infeasible), or a single outlier sits
near the boundary (the margin collapses). Fix: soft margin (Topic 73). Fails
when the true boundary is curved — fix: kernels (Topic 74).
Always scale features first.
Interview corner
Q. What exactly is the margin, and why maximise it?

The perpendicular distance from the hyperplane to the nearest training point of
either class; the "street" has width $2/\|w\|$. Maximising it maximises the
distance to the closest data, which bounds generalisation error and makes the
classifier robust to small perturbations of the inputs.
Q. Why $\frac12\|w\|^2$ instead of maximising $2/\|w\|$?

$2/\|w\|$ is non-convex and non-differentiable at 0. Since $t \mapsto 1/t$ is
monotone decreasing, maximising $2/\|w\|$ equals minimising $\|w\|$, and
squaring plus the $\frac12$ makes it a smooth convex quadratic whose gradient
is simply $w$ — ideal for QP solvers.
Q. Why label the classes $\pm1$?

It merges "correct side" and "how far" into one expression:
$y_i(w^Tx_i+b)\ge1$ handles both classes with one inequality. With $\{0,1\}$
you would need two separate cases.
Q. What is a support vector?

A training point with $\alpha_i>0$; equivalently one lying exactly on a margin
line, $y_i(w^Tx_i+b)=1$. They alone determine $w$. All other points can be
deleted without changing the model.
Q. Why derive the dual at all?

Two reasons. It exposes the sparsity (most $\alpha_i$ vanish, so the model is
compact and prediction is cheap). And it expresses everything through inner
products $\langle x_i,x_j\rangle$, which is the only reason the kernel trick
exists. The dual also has $n$ variables rather than $d$, so it is preferable
when features outnumber rows.
Q. Is the SVM solution unique?

The optimal $w$ is unique because the objective is strictly convex in $w$. The
set of $\alpha$ achieving it need not be unique when data points are duplicated
or collinear, but the resulting hyperplane is the same.
Q. What happens if the data is not linearly separable?

The hard-margin feasible set is empty and the problem has no solution. You must
either introduce slack variables (soft margin, Topic 73) or map to a space
where separation is possible (kernels, Topic 74).
Q. Is SVM affected by feature scaling?

Yes, strongly. The objective $\|w\|^2$ and the geometric margin are both
measured in feature units, so a large-range feature dominates. Always
standardise, inside a pipeline.
Q. How does SVM compare to logistic regression?

Logistic regression optimises log loss over all points, so every point
influences the boundary and it outputs calibrated probabilities. SVM optimises
hinge loss, so points beyond the margin contribute exactly zero, the solution
depends only on support vectors, and the output is a signed distance rather
than a probability. SVM tends to be better with few samples and many features;
logistic regression scales better and gives probabilities directly.
Worked Examples
The maximal margin for two points
Two training points: $x_1 = (1,1)$ with $y=-1$ and $x_2 = (3,3)$ with $y=+1$. A hard-margin SVM requires $y_i(w\cdot x_i + b) \ge 1$.
Step 1 – guess the form. By symmetry $w = (a,a)$. Both points must sit exactly on the margin (they are the support vectors):
-1\cdot(2a + b) = 1 \Rightarrow 2a+b = -1, \qquad +1\cdot(6a+b) = 1 \Rightarrow 6a+b = 1
Step 2 – solve. Subtracting: $4a = 2$, so $a = 0.5$ and $b = -2$. Therefore $w = (0.5,\,0.5)$, $b=-2$.
Step 3 – verify the margin constraints. At $(1,1)$: $0.5+0.5-2 = -1$. At $(3,3)$: $1.5+1.5-2 = +1$. Both are exactly on the margin.

Maximising the width is the same as minimising $\tfrac12\|w\|^2$ subject to the constraints, which is the SVM's quadratic program.
